text:
B: Hiya! Can you hear me alright, love?
A: Yeah, loud and clear. Hello. I'm Darren.
B: Darren! Oh, that's funny. My husband's called Darren. Well, sort of ex-husband. We're separated, never got round to the divorce.
A: Ha, hopefully I'm not putting you off, then.
B: No, no, he's alright, we get on fine. I'm Nicola, anyway. Where are you?
A: Kesgrave, near Ipswich. Suffolk. You?
B: St Helens, between Liverpool and Wigan. I'll be honest, I looked at your photo and thought, he looks like my dad or one of my brothers. Just a normal bloke who knows what he's doing.
A: I'll take that, to be fair. I said you reminded me of my wife, Karen, so we're even.
B: Oh, bless you. What do you do, then?
A: Gas engineer. Boilers, mainly. Got my own business, one van, about fourteen years now.
B: Ooh, I could do with you. Mine makes this horrible banging noise when the heating first comes on. The housing association sent someone and he said it was normal.
A: Banging? Could be air in the system, or a bit of sludge in the pipes. It's not dangerous usually, but it's not normal either. I'd get them back out, if I'm honest.
B: See, I knew it. I'll ring them. Do you like it, the job?
A: Yeah, I do. It's good money if you put the hours in. Winter's mad, everyone's boiler packs up the first cold week. My knees don't thank me, mind.
B: Oh, I know all about knees. I've got rheumatoid arthritis, so I've been off work about four years now. I was a carer in a residential home before that. I miss it, you know, the people.
A: That's a shame. That's a proper job, caring. Harder than mine, probably.
B: Ah, I don't know about that. You're the one lying on kitchen floors.
A: Ha, true. I'm hoping to get an apprentice in, so I can do more quoting and less crawling about.
B: That's sensible. My dad worked at the glassworks his whole life and his back was knackered by fifty. So you look after yourself.
A: Yeah, my dad was a lorry driver, same sort of thing. Wrecked by the end. I've done a bit better than him, I think. Bigger house, my own van, you know. That means something.
B: Course it does. He'd be proud of you, I bet. Was he an Ipswich fan?
A: Oh yeah, that's where I got it from. Do you follow anything?
B: Rugby league, half-heartedly. Saints, 'cause of my dad. I'll have the Challenge Cup final on, but I couldn't tell you the league table.
A: That's like my missus with the football. She sits there on her phone the whole match.
B: Ha, that'd be me. I'd have a book on my knee. How many kids have you got?
A: Two. Jess is twenty-one, moved to Colchester with her boyfriend last year. And Callum's seventeen, learning to drive. Costing me a fortune.
B: Oh, do you miss your Jess?
A: Erm, yeah. More than I'd tell her, to be fair. She's round most Sundays, though, for a roast.
B: Ah, that's lovely. Mine are fifteen and twelve, so I've got all that to come. Anyway, I'm waffling, sorry.
A: No, you're alright. I think that's us nearly done, actually.
B: Already? It's been lovely talking to you, Darren.
A: You too, Nicola. Get that boiler looked at, yeah.
